procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated May 22, 1968, of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 2636 of 1967 connected with Criminal Appeal No. 260
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The trial court convicted six accused of offences under sections 148 and 302 and 307 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). On appeal, the Allahabad High Court acquitted two of the accused. The High Court maintained the convictions of the remaining accused (the appellants) for offences under sections 148 and 34/426 I.P.C. The High Court directed the sentences to run concurrently.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused (appellants) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the judgment of the Allahabad High Court.

directions: The sentences on each of them are directed to run concurrently.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants under sections 148, 304 read with 149, and 307 read with 149 of the Indian Penal Code can be sustained when the charge specifically named only six individuals as members of the unlawful assembly, and two of them were acquitted.

facts: Six specific individuals were charged with forming an unlawful assembly under sections 148, 304 read with 149, and 307 read with 149 of the Indian Penal Code.
The charge explicitly named these six individuals as being the only members of the unlawful assembly.
On appeal, two of the six accused were acquitted.
This left only four individuals convicted as members of the assembly.
law: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code imposes constructive (or vicarious) liability on members of an unlawful assembly.
For a group to be considered an unlawful assembly under Section 141, it must consist of five or more persons.
Therefore, to convict an accused under Section 149, the court must find with certainty that there were at least five people sharing a common object.

An exception exists where fewer than five people can be convicted if the court is certain that five or more were present, but the identity of the other members is in doubt. This exception does not apply when the charge specifically names all the members and some are acquitted.
application: The Court applied the legal requirement of a minimum of five members to the facts of the case.

Since the charge specifically named only six individuals as constituting the entire unlawful assembly, the acquittal of two of them meant that the prosecution had only proven the involvement of four people.
With only four proven members, the group no longer met the legal definition of an unlawful assembly.
Because the charge was specific and did not allege the presence of other, unidentified persons, the court could not use the exception to uphold the conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the number of proven members of the assembly fell below the statutory minimum of five, the legal basis for an unlawful assembly was not established. Consequently, the convictions of the remaining four appellants under sections 148 (rioting) and 304/307 read with 149 (constructive liability) could not be sustained and were rejected.

issue.issue_text: Whether a conviction can be altered to be under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code when the original charge was under Section 149.

facts: Six accused were specifically named in a charge as being the only members of an unlawful assembly.
They were charged with offenses under sections 148, 302, and 307, all read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
On appeal, two of the six accused were acquitted.
This left only four individuals convicted of the offenses.
law: A conviction under Section 149 of the IPC requires the existence of an "unlawful assembly."
An "unlawful assembly," as defined in Section 141 of the IPC, must consist of five or more persons.
Section 34 of the IPC deals with criminal acts done by several persons in furtherance of a common intention and does not have a minimum number requirement.
application: The Supreme Court noted that since the charge specifically named only six people as members of the unlawful assembly, and two of them were acquitted, the number of convicted persons fell to four.
With only four people, the legal requirement of five or more members for an unlawful assembly was no longer met.
Consequently, the Court determined that the conviction of the remaining four appellants under Section 149 could not be sustained.
However, the Court found that the evidence clearly showed the appellants were guilty of the offenses (under Sections 304 and 307) committed in furtherance of a common intention.
Therefore, the Court altered the conviction from being read with Section 149 to being read with Section 34.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the conviction under Section 149 IPC was unsustainable because the number of convicted persons fell below the statutory minimum of five. It therefore set aside that conviction and substituted it with a conviction for the same substantive offenses read with Section 34 IPC, which does not require a minimum number of persons.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a charge specifically names all the individuals as being the only members of an unlawful assembly, and subsequent acquittals reduce the number of convicted persons to fewer than five, a conviction for an offense read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code cannot be sustained. In such a case, a conviction for a substantive offense read with Section 34 (common intention) can be substituted.
obiter: Since two of the accused had been totally acquitted of all charges and the others have been -acquitted of the charge of murder and there is no appeal ·against these acquittals we are unable to say whether these findings by the High Court are justified.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Although the conviction under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (unlawful assembly) cannot be sustained because the charge specifically named only six individuals and the acquittal of two brought the number below the required minimum of five, the evidence on record clearly establishes a common intention among the remaining appellants. The facts show they were the aggressors, came together armed with weapons, and acted in concert to demolish a thatch, using force when resisted. Therefore, the conviction is properly altered to be under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (common intention), and the appellants are held guilty for the substantive offences.
legal_tests_applied: To sustain a conviction under Section 149 IPC, the court must find with certainty that there were at least five persons sharing the common object. If a charge specifically names the members of the unlawful assembly and acquittals reduce the number of convicted persons to fewer than five, the conviction under Section 149 cannot be sustained.

A conviction can be altered from Section 149 IPC to Section 34 IPC if the evidence on record is sufficient to establish a common intention among the accused to commit the criminal act. Common intention can be inferred from the totality of the circumstances, including the accused acting as aggressors, coming together armed, and their collective actions in furtherance of their object.
why_appellant_lost: Despite successfully arguing that the conviction under Section 149 IPC was legally unsustainable, the appellants lost because the court found the evidence was sufficient to prove a 'common intention' under Section 34 IPC.

The court found clear evidence that the appellants were the aggressors, had a pre-existing dispute, came together armed with weapons (Karpa, Ballams, lathis, Bahangi), and acted in concert to demolish the victim's property and attack those who resisted.

The court relied on a dying declaration and eyewitness testimony which established that the appellants initiated the violence after being asked to stop pulling down the thatch, which demonstrated their shared intent to use force to achieve their objective.
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded in upholding the appellants' guilt because the court agreed to substitute the flawed conviction under Section 149 with a conviction under Section 34, based on the same evidence.

The court found that the evidence, which included prior threats, the nature of the weapons carried, and the consistent testimony of witnesses and a dying declaration, clearly indicated a common intention among the appellants to demolish the thatch and use force if necessary.
The court concluded that the appellants' actions were not a result of a sudden quarrel but a planned aggressive act, thereby justifying their conviction for the offences read with Section 34 IPC.
